episode.lensDescription: Everything filtered through how it affects actual students.
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Tuesday, March twenty-fourth. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation today, Alabama A&M University has been selected as one of five regional lead institutions nationwide for Amazon Web Services Machine Learning University. According to Alabama A&M University, the institution joins Delaware State University, Howard University, City Colleges of Chicago, and Oklahoma City Community College in this designation.

The selection follows Alabama A&M's hosting of a national gathering of Historically Black Colleges and Universities focused on artificial intelligence. As a regional lead, Alabama A&M will provide access to Amazon's industry-leading machine learning curriculum used to train Amazon engineers, along with low-cost cloud computing resources.

Faculty will receive professional development, lesson-planning support, course playbooks, and cloud credits to strengthen classroom instruction and advance research initiatives. The program addresses the national shortage of technology talent while expanding access for students historically underrepresented in computer science fields.

Programs under the regional lead designation are scheduled to launch in the upcoming academic year, with faculty training beginning this summer and student enrollment in courses to follow in the fall semester.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers today, University of Tennessee students express divided opinions about artificial intelligence's role in the workplace. According to WVLT, some embrace the technology as a business tool while others worry about misuse. The Boyd Center for Business and Economic Development found that about two-thirds of Tennessee businesses surveyed are using A.I. alongside their employees.

Don Bruce from the Boyd Center advised students to develop A.I. fluency to remain competitive, stating that A.I.-fluent candidates will be really sought after by employers. However, student reactions varied significantly, with one saying they felt a little bit worried about it and another noting the general population isn't using it for its good purposes.

The University's College of Emerging and Collaborative Studies has responded by launching an applied A.I. undergraduate degree and working with a robot named Pepper for hands-on learning. The department reports more than two hundred thirty students enrolled in their degree programs, with over fourteen hundred students taking classes involving A.I. and technology learning.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Practical Tips, philosophy professor Tom Feeney at the University of St. Thomas teaches students to use artificial intelligence as a critic that challenges arguments and exposes weak points rather than as a writing substitute. According to the University of St. Thomas newsroom, Feeney, who directs the Master of Arts in Artificial Intelligence Leadership program, said the failure mode with artificial intelligence is just turning over your agency and your creativity to it.

In his A.I. Ethics course, students complete multi-part papers analyzing technology through risk, virtue, and real-world consequences, with discussion and revision built into the process. The MAIL program launched in fall twenty twenty-five as a ten-course asynchronous online degree targeting professionals who want to integrate A.I. in their workplaces.

Feeney intentionally designed it as a Master of Arts rather than Master of Science, bringing together disciplines from ethics and history to business and law across three colleges. Student Dominic Adkins said the class initially convinced students that A.I. was going to destroy the world before examining the technology's limitations in the second half.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Alabama A&M Named Regional Lead for Amazon Machine Learning University
leadStory.summary: According to Alabama A&M University, the institution has been selected as one of five regional lead institutions nationwide for Amazon Web Services–Machine Learning University, joining Delaware State University, Howard University, City Colleges of Chicago, and Oklahoma City Community College. The designation follows AAMU's hosting of a national gathering of Historically Black Colleges and Universities focused on artificial intelligence. As a regional lead, AAMU will provide access to Amazon's industry-leading machine learning curriculum used to train Amazon engineers, along with low-cost cloud computing resources through Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab. Faculty will receive professional development, lesson-planning support, course playbooks, and AWS cloud credits to strengthen classroom instruction and advance research initiatives. The program addresses the national shortage of technology talent while expanding access for students historically underrepresented in computer science fields. Dr. Margie Vela from AWS noted that HBCUs "continue to lead at the forefront of A.I. innovation" and are "not simply participating in the A.I. future — they are defining it." Programs under the regional lead designation are scheduled to launch in the upcoming academic year, with faculty training beginning this summer and student enrollment in AWS-MLU courses to follow in the fall semester.

quickHits.headline: St. Thomas Professor Advocates A.I. as Critical Thinking Tool
quickHits.summary: According to the University of St. Thomas newsroom, philosophy professor Tom Feeney teaches students to use artificial intelligence as a critic that challenges arguments and exposes weak points rather than as a writing substitute. Feeney, who directs the Master of Arts in Artificial Intelligence Leadership program, said the "failure mode with artificial intelligence is just turning over your agency and your creativity to it." In his A.I. Ethics course, students complete multi-part papers analyzing technology through risk, virtue, and real-world consequences, with discussion and revision built into the process. The MAIL program launched in fall 2025 as a 10-course asynchronous online degree targeting professionals who want to integrate A.I. in their workplaces. Feeney intentionally designed it as a Master of Arts rather than Master of Science, bringing together disciplines from ethics and history to business and law across three colleges. Student Dominic Adkins said the class initially convinced students that "A.I. was going to destroy the world" before examining the technology's limitations in the second half. Feeney uses A.I. personally for tasks like scaling recipes and car repairs but draws boundaries, noting he "wouldn't turn the core work of raising children over to A.I. just yet."
